name: AI for Community Advocacy
objectives: Given a community concern, write a one-sentence problem statement and a specific ask that says what, from whom and by when, shaped with at least two people affected
For your issue, find facts from official or trusted sources and collect community stories, with three facts each listed with source, link and date, and stories shared only with permission
Using official websites, identify the decision maker, the next meeting or comment deadline, your allies and likely opposition, with the decision maker confirmed on an official source
Using your checked facts and a story, write a respectful letter or public comment that makes your ask, in under 300 words with who you are, facts, a story and the ask
Using AI for text and a free design tool, create a one-page fact sheet with the ask in a clear box, so a reader can tell you the ask after one minute
At a public meeting, give a two-minute testimony and plan supporter action within nonprofit advocacy rules, timed at two minutes or less and with no support for candidates

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Defining the issue and your ask
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a community concern into a clear problem statement and a specific ask.
This lesson builds toward: Given a community concern, you will write a one-sentence problem statement and a specific ask that says what, from whom and by when, shaped with at least two people affected.
Big concerns like "our neighborhood isn't safe" are hard for officials to act on. Narrow it to a specific problem: "Children cross six lanes on Main Street at 5th Avenue to reach school, and there is no crosswalk signal."
Then make a specific ask: what exactly you want, from whom, by when. "We ask the City Transportation Department to install a pedestrian signal at Main and 5th before next school year." A clear ask gives decision makers something to say yes to.
Ask AI to sharpen it: "Help me turn this concern into a one-sentence problem and a specific, realistic ask: [your concern]." Then check it with the people most affected. Advocacy works best when the community shapes the ask.
Step by step:
- Write the concern in your own words.
- Narrow it to one specific problem, place and group affected.
- Write an ask: what, who decides, by when.
- Ask AI to sharpen the wording.
- Check it with people most affected.
Words to know:
- Advocacy: speaking up to change a policy, practice or decision.
- Ask: the specific action you want a decision maker to take.
- Problem statement: one or two sentences describing the issue clearly.
Try it now: Pick a real local concern. Write a one-sentence problem and a specific ask, use AI to sharpen them, and share them with two people affected.
You can now turn a concern into a clear problem statement and a specific ask.

check.q: What three things does a strong ask include?
options: Your name, age and address
What, from whom and by when
A slogan, a logo and a color
A complaint, a threat and a deadline
check.why: A strong ask names the action, the decision maker and the deadline.

check.q: Your group's concern is "our neighborhood is unsafe." What would you do first?
options: Narrow it to one specific problem officials can act on
Send it to every official in the state
Post it online without changes
Wait for things to get worse
check.why: Specific problems lead to specific actions officials can take.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Researching facts and checking sources
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find facts that support your case and check every one against an official or trusted source.
This lesson builds toward: For your issue, you will find facts from official or trusted sources and collect community stories, with three facts each listed with source, link and date, and stories shared only with permission.
Facts make officials listen. Useful sources: city and county websites, meeting minutes and budgets, state agencies, the U.S. Census Bureau (data.census.gov) for population and income data, police or transportation data, local news, and university or nonprofit research.
AI can suggest where to look and what to search for: "What kinds of public data would show pedestrian safety problems at an intersection in a U.S. city, and where would I find them?" But AI can invent statistics and studies. Never use a number from AI unless you find it yourself in the original source.
Collect three strong facts, each with the source name, link and date. Add real stories: a parent, a student, a crossing guard. Always get permission to share someone's story, and leave out private details they do not want public.
Step by step:
- Ask AI where to find data on your issue.
- Go to those sources yourself.
- Write down three facts with source, link and date.
- Never use a number you cannot find in the original source.
- Collect two stories with permission.
Words to know:
- Source: where a fact comes from.
- Primary source: the original place data or information was published.
- Meeting minutes: the official written record of a public meeting.
Official sources:
- U.S. Census Bureau: data.census.gov
Try it now: Find three facts about your issue from official or trusted sources, with link and date for each. Ask two people if you may share their story.
You can now research checked facts and gather community stories with permission.

check.q: What is a trusted source for a fact about your city?
options: A random social media post
An AI answer with no link
The city's own official website or report
A rumor from a neighbor
check.why: Official sources are where facts can be checked and cited.

check.q: A neighbor tells you a powerful story about being hurt at the crosswalk. What would you do before using it?
options: Use it with their full name and address
Change the details and use it anyway
Post it online first
Ask their permission and how they want to be named
check.why: Stories are shared only with the person's permission.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding the decision maker and the right moment
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify who can say yes to your ask and when they will decide.
This lesson builds toward: Using official websites, you will identify the decision maker, the next meeting or comment deadline, your allies and likely opposition, with the decision maker confirmed on an official source.
Advocacy fails when it goes to the wrong person. Find out who has the power to say yes: a city council member, a county board, a school board, a state legislator, a department head or a company manager.
Ask AI: "In a typical U.S. city, who decides whether a new crosswalk signal is installed, and what process is involved?" Then confirm on your own city's website, or call the office. Learn the calendar: when budgets are set, when the council or board meets, and when public comment is open.
Map your allies (neighbors, schools, churches, businesses, other nonprofits) and anyone likely to oppose, and why. Allies make you stronger; understanding opposition helps you answer concerns.
Step by step:
- Ask AI who typically decides on your issue.
- Confirm on your local government's website or by phone.
- Find meeting dates, budget timing and public comment periods.
- List allies and likely opposition.
- Pick your moment to act.
Words to know:
- Decision maker: the person or body with the power to say yes to your ask.
- Public comment: a chance for the public to speak or write to officials before a decision.
- Ally: a person or group that supports your cause.
Try it now: Find the decision maker for your issue and their next meeting or comment deadline on an official website. List three allies and one likely concern from opponents.
You can now find the right decision maker, timing and allies for an advocacy ask.

check.q: Who is a decision maker in advocacy?
options: The person or body who can say yes to your ask
Anyone who agrees with you
The newspaper
The person who complains the loudest
check.why: The decision maker has the power to grant your ask.

check.q: You want a new park light, but you do not know who decides. What would you do?
options: Write to the President
Check the city website or call the city to find out
Guess and send it to the school board
Wait until someone tells you
check.why: Confirm the decision maker on an official source before you reach out.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a letter or public comment with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short, respectful letter or public comment that makes your ask.
This lesson builds toward: Using your checked facts and a story, you will write a respectful letter or public comment that makes your ask, in under 300 words with who you are, facts, a story and the ask.
A strong letter or comment is short (under 300 words) and has four parts: who you are and your connection to the issue, the problem with one or two facts, a short real story, and your specific ask with a thank-you.
Ask AI: "Write a respectful public comment under 300 words to the City Council. I am a parent at Lincoln Elementary. Problem: [problem]. Facts: [your checked facts]. Story: [shared with permission]. Ask: [your ask]." Then edit so it sounds like you.
Personal letters beat form letters: officials notice when hundreds of identical AI messages arrive. Encourage supporters to add their own sentence. Stay respectful even if you are angry; insults get ignored.
Step by step:
- Who you are and your connection.
- The problem with one or two checked facts.
- A short real story, shared with permission.
- Your specific ask and a thank-you.
- Edit it to sound like you; keep it under 300 words.
Words to know:
- Form letter: the same letter sent by many people with little or no change.
- Constituent: a person who lives in an official's district and whom they represent.
Try it now: Write a letter or public comment of under 300 words for your issue with AI help, using your checked facts and a story shared with permission. Read it out loud and edit it.
You can now write a short, respectful letter or public comment that makes a clear ask.

options: A staff member of a nonprofit
A paid lobbyist
A newspaper reporter
A person who lives in an official's district
check.why: Officials pay attention to the people they represent.

check.q: AI writes a letter that sounds angry and blames the council. What would you do?
options: Send it to show how upset you are
Rewrite it to be respectful, with facts, a story and the ask
Add more angry words
Send the same letter from 100 fake names
check.why: Respectful, personal letters with a clear ask are more likely to be heard.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making a one-page fact sheet
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a one-page fact sheet that busy officials and neighbors can read in a minute.
This lesson builds toward: Using AI for text and a free design tool, you will create a one-page fact sheet with the ask in a clear box, so a reader can tell you the ask after one minute.
A fact sheet is a one-page handout you leave with officials, share online and give to supporters. Busy people read the top and skim the rest.
Structure: a bold headline with the problem, three key facts with sources, a short quote or story, the ask in a box, and who you are with contact information. Use plain language, big text and one simple chart or photo if it helps.
Ask AI to draft the text from your facts, then lay it out in Canva or Google Docs. Check every number and source again. Translate it if your community speaks other languages; AI can draft a translation, but have a fluent speaker check it.
Step by step:
- Write a headline that names the problem.
- Add three facts with sources.
- Add one short quote or story.
- Put the ask in a box.
- Lay it out on one page; check numbers; get translations checked by fluent speakers.
Words to know:
- Fact sheet: a one-page handout summarizing an issue, facts and an ask.
- Plain language: clear, simple writing most people can understand.
Try it now: Make a one-page fact sheet for your issue with AI drafting the text and Canva or Google Docs for layout. Ask someone to read it in one minute and tell you the ask.
You can now create a clear one-page fact sheet for an advocacy issue.

check.q: Who is a fact sheet mainly for?
options: Busy officials and neighbors who need the key points fast
Only the people who wrote it
Lawyers in court
Students writing essays
check.why: A fact sheet gives busy readers the problem, facts and ask in one minute.

check.q: Your draft fact sheet is two full pages of small text. What would you do?
options: Make the text smaller
Add a third page for more facts
Cut it to one page with the ask in a clear box
Remove the ask to save space
check.why: One page with a clear ask is easier to read and act on.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Public testimony, supporters and the rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Give a two-minute testimony, mobilize supporters and follow nonprofit advocacy rules.
This lesson builds toward: At a public meeting, you will give a two-minute testimony and plan supporter action within nonprofit advocacy rules, timed at two minutes or less and with no support for candidates.
Many councils and boards give each speaker two or three minutes. Prepare a two-minute version of your letter: about 250 spoken words. Ask AI to trim it, then practice out loud with a timer. Start with your name and connection, end with your ask, and bring copies of your fact sheet.
Bring supporters. A room of neighbors wearing the same color sends a message. Use AI to draft a short sign-up message and reminders, and help supporters write their own comments.
Know the rules for nonprofits. The IRS says a 501(c)(3) may do some lobbying, but not as a substantial part of its activities, and educating the public on policy is not lobbying. It is absolutely prohibited from supporting or opposing candidates for office, though nonpartisan voter education and registration are allowed. Ask a nonprofit lawyer or your state's nonprofit association about specifics.
Step by step:
- Trim your letter to about 250 spoken words.
- Practice out loud with a two-minute timer.
- Bring fact sheet copies and supporters.
- Use AI to draft sign-up and reminder messages.
- Check the nonprofit rules on lobbying and candidates.
Words to know:
- Testimony: speaking to officials at a public meeting about an issue.
- Lobbying: trying to influence legislation, such as contacting lawmakers about a bill.
- Nonpartisan: not supporting any political party or candidate.
Official sources:
- IRS: Lobbying
- IRS: Restriction of political campaign intervention by 501(c)(3) organizations
Try it now: Final task: trim your letter into a two-minute testimony and practice it out loud with a timer. Put it together with your problem and ask, facts, stories, decision maker, letter and fact sheet to complete your advocacy kit.
You can now plan and carry out a small, fact-based advocacy campaign with AI help, within the rules.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Problem and ask The problem is too broad, or the ask is missing what, from whom or by when. A one-sentence problem and a specific ask with what, from whom and by when. Shows how people affected helped shape the ask. Facts and stories A fact has no source, or a story is used without permission. Three facts with source, link and date, and two stories shared with permission. Facts come from primary sources and stories use the names people chose. Decision maker Wrong or unconfirmed decision maker. Decision maker and next deadline confirmed on an official website. Also lists allies and an answer to the main opposition concern. Letter or comment and fact sheet Over 300 words, disrespectful, or no clear ask. Under 300 words, respectful, with who you are, facts, a story and the ask; the fact sheet fits on one page. A reader can say the ask after one minute with the fact sheet. Testimony and rules Over two minutes, not practiced, or mentions support for a candidate. Practiced out loud in two minutes or less, starting with name and connection, and issue-only. Includes a plan for supporters to attend or comment. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Supporting one party
Paid for by the government
Not supporting any candidate or party
Against all officials
check.why: Nonpartisan means not taking sides with candidates or parties.

check.q: Your testimony runs three and a half minutes, but you have two. What would you do?
options: Speak faster
Keep going when the timer ends
Skip the ask
Cut it to your name, connection, one fact, one story and the ask, and practice with a timer
check.why: Trimming to the key parts and practicing keeps you within the time limit.
